week_in_brief: A week for rewarding the right behavior, not just the purchase — and giving your staff the tools to keep pace with shoppers who now expect instant answers.

items.headline: Google Stopped Caring About Your Keywords — Your Loyalty Program Still Does
items.whats_happening: Google's paid search platform is moving away from strict keyword bidding toward intent and creative relevance. At the same time, the strongest retail loyalty programs — airlines, casinos, hospitality — are designed to reward behavioral change (repeat visits, cross-category purchases, status progression) rather than just transactions. Both shifts point to the same reality: you can't buy relevance with volume anymore; you have to design for it.
items.so_what: Audit whether your loyalty program rewards frequency or just spending, and whether your paid search campaigns rely on generic ad copy and weak landing pages. In both cases, the winners are the ones who connect the dots across touchpoints and guide customers through intentional journeys.

items.headline: Ace Hardware Gave Store Associates an AI Assistant — And Shoppers Are Still Choosing Human Help
items.whats_happening: Ace Hardware deployed Hey ARMA, an AI-powered assistant that gives red-vested associates instant access to product details, project guidance, and recommendations while on the floor. It's now live in 2,300+ stores. Meanwhile, Samsung research shows 68% of shoppers still prefer human interaction over AI — but only if that human has the information they need, right when they need it. Mobile devices and AI tools aren't replacing staff; they're making them faster and more confident.
items.so_what: If your associates are walking customers to a kiosk or a back office to look something up, you're losing conversions. Equipping staff with mobile tools that provide instant inventory visibility and product intelligence is a low-risk investment with measurable ROI in basket size and customer experience. The hardware chain figured it out — so can you.

items.headline: Consumers Are Trading Down — But They're Paying Up for Loyalty Programs That Show Progress
items.whats_happening: Financial pressure is reshaping spending behavior: shoppers are buying less, switching to private label, and gravitating toward retailers with visible value (not just discounts). At the same time, 79% of consumers are enrolled in at least one paid loyalty program, and 81% say they're motivated by seeing their progress toward rewards — the tier, the gap, the milestone. The contradiction is clarifying: people will cut spending everywhere except the programs that make them feel invested.
items.so_what: Free loyalty programs with birthday coupons and generic point-stacking aren't retaining customers in this environment. Paid membership with visible progression, member-only pricing, and status recognition is. If your program doesn't give customers a reason to come back beyond saving a few dollars, it's not a loyalty program — it's a coupon delivery system.

items.headline: Retail Media Teams Are Finally Talking to Merchandising — And It's Paying Off
items.whats_happening: Ace Hardware's retail media network launched with one non-negotiable requirement: merchandising and media teams had to move together from day one. Most retail media operations remain siloed — media sells ads, merchants manage inventory, and neither fully trusts the other's priorities. Ace's approach was to prove business impact first (real-time, measurable results), which earned merchant buy-in without forcing org chart surgery. The lesson: alignment isn't a process change; it's a proof-of-value change.
items.so_what: If you're building or operating a retail media network, your media team and your merchandising team need to share goals, data, and decision-making. If they're not already in the same room, start there. Proof beats politics.

this_weeks_take: The thread running through all of this: relevance is designed, not bought. Whether you're bidding on search ads, running a loyalty program, or equipping your staff with AI tools, the brands winning right now are the ones building systems that connect behavior, data, and experience across every touchpoint. Generic doesn't cut it anymore.
